questions.stem: Which list puts these parts of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency?
options: Microwave, radio, visible, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma, X-ray
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
Gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, infrared, microwave, visible, X-ray, ultraviolet, gamma
questions.explanation: Radio waves have the lowest frequencies and longest wavelengths, and gamma rays the highest frequencies and shortest wavelengths. The reverse list is in order of increasing wavelength, not frequency.

questions.stem: What do all electromagnetic waves have in common in a vacuum?
options: They all need a medium of particles to carry their energy
They all have the same wavelength but different speeds
They all travel at the same speed, about 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
They all have the same frequency but different wavelengths
questions.explanation: Every electromagnetic wave, from radio to gamma, travels through a vacuum at c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. They differ in frequency and wavelength, and none of them needs a medium.

questions.stem: How are electromagnetic waves modelled?
options: As transverse waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields
As longitudinal waves of compressions and rarefactions in air
As transverse waves of particles vibrating in the medium
As longitudinal waves of oscillating electric fields only
questions.explanation: An electromagnetic wave is a transverse wave of electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. Because the fields need no particles, the wave crosses a vacuum.

questions.stem: A mobile phone inside a sealed jar keeps receiving calls as the air is pumped out, but the sound of its ringtone fades. Why?
options: Radio waves are electromagnetic and cross a vacuum; sound is mechanical and needs a medium
Radio waves travel faster than sound, so they can escape before the air is removed
Sound waves are electromagnetic and are absorbed by the glass walls of the jar
Radio waves are longitudinal, so they can pass through gaps that sound cannot
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles to pass on its vibrations, so it fades as the air is removed. The phone's signal is an electromagnetic wave, which travels through a vacuum.

questions.stem: A Wi-Fi router transmits at 2.4 GHz. What is the wavelength of these waves in air? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/(2.4 × 10⁹) = 0.125 m. Forgetting the 'giga' (10⁹) gives very wrong answers, and multiplying c by f gives 7.2 × 10¹⁷ m.

questions.stem: Green light has a wavelength of 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m in a vacuum. What is its frequency? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 6.0 × 10¹² Hz
6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Dividing λ by c gives the period, 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ s, not the frequency.

questions.stem: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum is used to make images of broken bones?
options: Microwaves
Radio waves
X-rays
Infrared
questions.explanation: X-rays pass easily through soft tissue but are absorbed more by bone, so bones show up on the image. Infrared is used in thermal imaging, and microwaves and radio waves in communications.

questions.stem: A thermal imaging camera shows warm bodies glowing at night. Which radiation does it detect?
options: Microwaves
Infrared
Ultraviolet
Gamma rays
questions.explanation: All warm objects emit infrared radiation, and warmer objects emit more, so an infrared camera can show people and animals in darkness. Ultraviolet and gamma rays are not emitted in useful amounts by objects at body temperature.

questions.stem: Why is ultraviolet radiation more harmful to skin than visible light?
options: It is a mechanical wave, so it carries energy by vibrating the skin
Its higher frequency carries more energy, enough to damage cells and DNA
Its longer wavelength lets it penetrate deeper into the body's organs
It travels faster than visible light, so it strikes the skin harder
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency than visible light, and higher-frequency radiation carries more energy per photon, enough to damage skin cells and DNA. Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength than visible light, and all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.

questions.stem: Light from the Sun travels 1.50 × 10¹¹ m to reach Earth. How long does it take? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: t = d/v = 1.50 × 10¹¹/3.00 × 10⁸ = 500 s, a little over 8 minutes. Dividing the speed by the distance gives 2.0 × 10⁻³, which has the wrong units.

questions.stem: Using the ray model, what does the law of reflection state?
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the surface
The angle of reflection is always half the angle of incidence for a flat mirror
The reflected ray always leaves at right angles to the reflecting surface
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
questions.explanation: The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane, and the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. Both are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface.

questions.stem: What is refraction?
options: The bouncing of a wave off a boundary back into the first medium
The spreading of a wave as it passes through a narrow gap
A change in the frequency of a wave as it enters a new medium
A change in the direction of a wave caused by a change in its speed
questions.explanation: Refraction is the change in direction of travel when a wave's speed changes, usually as it crosses into a different medium at an angle. The frequency stays the same; it is the speed and wavelength that change.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes at an angle from air into glass, where it travels more slowly. How does it bend?
options: Away from the normal, so the angle of refraction is larger than the angle of incidence
Along the surface, so the angle of refraction is exactly 90° to the normal
Not at all, because light keeps its direction when it slows down evenly
Towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence
questions.explanation: When light slows down on entering a medium at an angle it bends towards the normal. Leaving glass into air, where it speeds up, it bends away from the normal.

questions.stem: Light enters glass of refractive index 1.50. What is its speed in the glass? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The refractive index is n = c/v, so v = c/n = 3.00 × 10⁸/1.50 = 2.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Multiplying by n gives a speed faster than light in a vacuum, which is impossible.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters water of refractive index 1.33. What are its frequency and wavelength in the water?
options: Lower frequency; wavelength stays at 600 nm
Same frequency; wavelength about 451 nm
Same wavelength; frequency 1.33 times smaller
Same frequency; wavelength about 798 nm
questions.explanation: The frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary. The speed falls by a factor of 1.33, so from v = fλ the wavelength falls by the same factor: 600/1.33 ≈ 451 nm.

questions.stem: A ray in air strikes glass of refractive index 1.50 at an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of refraction? Use n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with n(air) = 1.00.
questions.explanation: sin θ₂ = (1.00 × sin 30°)/1.50 = 0.333, so θ₂ = 19.5°. Dividing the angle itself by 1.50 gives 20.0°, which is close but wrong because Snell's law relates the sines of the angles.

questions.stem: A ray passes from water (n = 1.33) into air (n = 1.00) with an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: sin θ₂ = 1.33 × sin 40°/1.00 = 0.855, so θ₂ ≈ 58.7°. The light speeds up as it leaves the water, so it bends away from the normal and the angle increases.

questions.stem: In an experiment, a ray in air enters a block at 45° to the normal and refracts at 28°. What is the refractive index of the block?
questions.explanation: n = sin 45°/sin 28° = 0.707/0.469 ≈ 1.51. Dividing the angles themselves gives 1.61, and inverting the ratio gives 0.66, which is less than 1 and impossible for a material.

questions.stem: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is when viewed from the side. Why?
options: Light from the bottom slows down as it passes from the water into the air
Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water
Light from the bottom bends towards the normal as it leaves the water
Light from the bottom is totally internally reflected at the water surface
questions.explanation: Rays from the bottom speed up as they leave the water, so they bend away from the normal. The eye traces them back in straight lines to a point above the true bottom, so the pool looks shallower. Light speeds up, not slows, when it enters air.

questions.stem: Why can you see your reflection in a mirror but not in a sheet of white paper, though both reflect most of the light?
options: The paper refracts the light inside it before reflecting it back
The paper's rough surface scatters parallel rays in many directions
The paper absorbs most of the light, so too little is reflected
The mirror's surface does not obey the law of reflection at all
questions.explanation: Each ray obeys the law of reflection at both surfaces, but the paper's surface is rough on a small scale, so the normals point in many directions and parallel rays scatter. This diffuse reflection forms no image, while the smooth mirror gives regular reflection.

questions.stem: White light passes through a glass prism and spreads into a spectrum. Why does violet light bend more than red light?
options: The glass's refractive index is higher for violet, so violet slows more
Violet light travels faster in glass, so it changes direction more
Violet light has a longer wavelength, so it diffracts more around the prism
The glass absorbs red light first, so only violet reaches the far side
questions.explanation: This is dispersion: the refractive index of glass depends on wavelength and is greater for violet than for red. Violet slows more and is refracted through a larger angle, separating the colours.

questions.stem: A ray inside a transparent block is totally internally reflected at its surface. Which two conditions must hold?
options: Light strikes a silvered surface at an angle equal to the critical angle
Light travels into a medium of lower refractive index, at more than the critical angle
Light travels into a medium of higher refractive index, at more than the critical angle
Light travels into a medium of lower refractive index, at less than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection happens only when light inside a denser medium meets a boundary with a less dense one, such as glass to air, at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. Then no light is refracted out; it is all reflected.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light passing from glass (n = 1.50) into air (n = 1.00)?
questions.explanation: At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary, so sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.00/1.50 = 0.667 and θc = 41.8°. The complement, 48.2°, is a common slip.

questions.stem: Light travels along an optical fibre with very little loss. What keeps it inside the glass core?
options: A reflective metal coating painted on the outside of the cladding
Total internal reflection, because the cladding has a lower refractive index
Total internal reflection, because the cladding has a higher refractive index
Refraction towards the normal each time the light strikes the cladding
questions.explanation: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding around it, so light striking the boundary beyond the critical angle is totally internally reflected again and again along the fibre.

questions.stem: A light ray inside a glass block (n = 1.50) strikes the glass-water boundary at 60°. Water has n = 1.33. What happens?
options: It is partly refracted into the water, because 60° is below the critical angle of about 62°
It is totally internally reflected, because 60° is above the critical angle of about 42°
It passes straight into the water without bending, because both are transparent
It is totally internally reflected, because water has a lower refractive index
questions.explanation: For glass to water, sin θc = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887, so θc ≈ 62.5°. 60° is less than this, so some light refracts into the water. 42° is the critical angle for glass to air, not glass to water.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the diffraction of light?
options: The change in direction of waves as they enter a new medium
The bouncing of waves back from a hard, smooth surface
The adding together of two waves that meet at one point
The spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or past an edge
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the bending or spreading of waves through an aperture or around an obstacle. A change of direction on entering a new medium is refraction.

questions.stem: When does light passing through a narrow slit spread out most?
options: When the light is bright and the slit is very wide
When the slit is made of a material that slows the light
When the slit width is close to the wavelength of the light
When the slit width is many times the wavelength of the light
questions.explanation: Diffraction is most noticeable when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength. Visible light has wavelengths below a micrometre, so only very narrow slits spread it noticeably.

questions.stem: A house behind a hill receives long-wavelength radio signals but not the shorter-wavelength signals from the same tower. Why?
options: Shorter wavelengths are reflected by the air before they reach the hill
Longer wavelengths refract more as they pass through the solid hill
Longer wavelengths diffract more around large obstacles such as hills
Longer wavelengths travel faster, so they reach further around the hill
questions.explanation: The amount of diffraction depends on the wavelength compared with the obstacle. Waves hundreds of metres long bend noticeably around a hill, while short waves travel in nearly straight lines and leave a shadow behind it.

questions.stem: Why can you hear someone around a corner but not see them?
options: Sound is a transverse wave and bends easily; light is longitudinal and cannot bend
Sound wavelengths are similar to doorway sizes, so sound diffracts; light's are far smaller
Sound travels faster than light, so it reaches around the corner first
Light is absorbed by air, but sound travels through air without loss
questions.explanation: Sound has wavelengths from centimetres to metres, comparable to doorways, so it spreads widely. Light's wavelength is about a million times smaller, so it hardly diffracts at all around everyday objects.

questions.stem: How is the plane of polarisation of an electromagnetic wave defined?
options: By the direction of travel and the direction of the wave's displacement
By the direction of travel and the direction of the oscillating electric field
By the direction of travel and the direction of the oscillating magnetic field
By the directions of the electric and magnetic fields, which are parallel
questions.explanation: The plane of polarisation contains the direction of travel and the oscillating electric field. The magnetic field oscillates at right angles to this plane.

questions.stem: Why can light be polarised but sound cannot?
options: Light is a longitudinal wave; sound in air is a transverse wave
Light is a transverse wave; sound in air is a longitudinal wave
Light travels much faster than sound in air and in other media
Light has a much shorter wavelength than sound in air
questions.explanation: Polarisation restricts the oscillation to a single plane, which only makes sense when the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of travel. Sound in air oscillates along its direction of travel, so it cannot be polarised.

questions.stem: Unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters. The second is rotated until no light gets through. What is the angle between their transmission axes?
questions.explanation: The first filter passes light polarised along its axis. When the second filter's axis is at 90° to this, it blocks that light completely. At 0° or 180° the axes are parallel and the most light passes.

questions.stem: Glare reflected from a flat road is mostly horizontally polarised. How should polarising sunglasses be designed to cut it?
options: With horizontal transmission axes, so the horizontally polarised glare is blocked
With transmission axes at 45°, so all of the glare passes through unchanged
With no particular orientation, because filters block all reflected light equally
With vertical transmission axes, so the horizontally polarised glare is blocked
questions.explanation: A polarising filter transmits light polarised along its axis and blocks light polarised at right angles to it. Vertical axes therefore block the horizontally polarised glare while letting through about half of the unpolarised light.

questions.stem: Light passing through a polarising filter can be blocked completely by a second filter. What does this show about light?
options: It is a transverse wave, oscillating at right angles to its direction of travel
It is a longitudinal wave, oscillating along its direction of travel
It is a mechanical wave, which needs particles in the filter to carry it
It is a stream of particles, which are too large to pass the second filter
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves have an oscillation direction that a filter can select and a second, crossed filter can block. A longitudinal wave oscillates along its direction of travel, so rotating a filter would make no difference to it.

questions.stem: Two tuning forks of slightly different frequency sound together, and the loudness rises and falls regularly. What is this called?
options: Beats, produced by superposition of the two waves
Resonance, produced by one fork forcing the other
Diffraction, produced by the waves spreading out
Refraction, produced by the waves changing speed
questions.explanation: Beats occur when two waves of slightly different frequency superpose. They drift in and out of phase, so the combined amplitude, and the loudness, rises and falls regularly.

questions.stem: Tuning forks of 440 Hz and 444 Hz are sounded together. What beat frequency is heard?
options: 884 Hz
2 Hz
4 Hz
442 Hz
questions.explanation: The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies: 444 − 440 = 4 Hz. The note heard has a pitch of about 442 Hz, the average, but it swells and fades 4 times a second.

questions.stem: A guitarist plays a string with a 330 Hz tuning fork and hears 3 beats per second. Tightening the string slightly makes the beats slower. What was the string's frequency?
options: 324 Hz
327 Hz
333 Hz
336 Hz
questions.explanation: 3 beats per second means the string was at 327 Hz or 333 Hz. Tightening raises a string's frequency; since the beats slowed, the frequency moved closer to 330 Hz, so it must have started below it, at 327 Hz.
